title: Hardware and the disk-space manager
lead: Follow one absent page into RAM, then calculate why two equal page counts can take different time.
goals: Trace the path from SQL down to pages
Calculate read costs using an explicitly stated model

sections.title: A requested row must reach the CPU before it can be tested
sections.html:
Suppose a query needs a student record on page 7, and that page is not in RAM. The CPU cannot test the stored age directly through the database's disk-page interface. It first needs the bytes in memory. A page is the chunk the DBMS manages for these transfers; one read can bring several records, including some the query will reject.

  1. Planning checks the SQL and chooses a way to compute its answer.
  2. Execution runs the chosen operations and asks file/index management for records.
  3. File/index management determines that the required record is on page 7.
  4. Buffer management checks its resident pages. Because page 7 is absent, it obtains space for it.
  5. Disk-space management maps page 7 to stored bytes and reads them into memory. Execution can now inspect the record.

If the next request needs another record on page 7 while it remains resident, the buffer can reuse it. That request still performs computation but avoids another disk read. Concurrency control and recovery span these responsibilities; a layer is a responsibility, not necessarily a separate operating-system process.

The storage hierarchy trades latency, capacity and persistence. CPU caches and ordinary RAM are fast but volatile: their contents disappear without power. HDDs and SSDs keep data persistently through a block interface, but reading them costs time. A disk-oriented DBMS keeps its persistent database on storage and processes pages in RAM, so the database can exceed RAM capacity. An in-memory design still needs a durability strategy.

On an HDD, a new-location read moves a head (seek), waits for rotation, then transfers bytes. An SSD has no mechanical head, but its physical flash read/program/erase units need not equal a DBMS page. These differences matter when turning a count of page operations into a time estimate.

Try: two qualifying records share page 7. Must finding two records require two disk reads?

No. One page read can bring both records into RAM. If the page remains resident, the second record can be inspected there. Record count, page count and disk-read count are different quantities.

Is a DBMS page necessarily one NAND erase block?

No. The DBMS page is a logical I/O unit; the device has its own physical program and erase units.

sections.title: Pay for positioning once or two hundred times?
sections.html:
Use an original simplified HDD model, not a measured machine: seek=4 ms, rotational delay=3 ms, and transfer of one page=0.1 ms. A random uncached page read therefore costs 4+3+0.1=7.1 ms. The large part is finding the bytes, not transferring the page.

Read patternPositioningTransferTotal
1 random page4+3=7 ms0.1 ms7.1 ms
200 serial random pages200×7=1400 ms200×0.1=20 ms1420 ms
200 contiguous pages in one uninterrupted run7 ms once200×0.1=20 ms27 ms

The random case assumes every request needs fresh positioning; there are no cache hits, parallel I/O or read-ahead. The continuous sequential case shares its initial positioning and ignores track changes, pauses and other overheads. Both read 200 pages, but their modelled durations differ by 1420/27≈52.6. This ratio follows from the assumptions; it is not a universal speedup and should not be copied to an SSD.

Why does a larger continuous run help? The initial 7 ms buys access to the start of the run. Each further page adds only 0.1 ms in this idealised model. For two pages, the totals are 14.2 ms random versus 7.2 ms continuous; the benefit is smaller because there are fewer later pages sharing that initial cost. Prefetching requests expected pages ahead of use and can overlap work, but its costs and wrong predictions must also be counted.

Try: calculate ten random pages and one ten-page continuous run.

Random: 10×7.1=71 ms. Continuous: 7+10×0.1=8 ms. Both transfer ten pages; repeated positioning accounts for the 63 ms difference under the model.

Key takeaway

Random reads repeat positioning costs; a continuous run shares the initial cost. This explains the difference between 1420 ms and 27 ms in the exercise. The numbers depend on the stated assumptions and are not a universal HDD or SSD speedup.

Why does the model charge 200 seeks for random reads but one for the continuous run?

Each random request repositions. The continuous scan shares the initial positioning under the stated idealized assumptions.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 15–19. Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: Turn a page ID into an address
sections.html:
The buffer asks for page 7, not for an application-specific filename and hard-coded address. To see what the disk-space layer must resolve, use an original layout: pages are 4096 bytes, numbering begins at 0, and the file has no header.

page 0 begins at      0
page 1 begins at   4096
page 2 begins at   8192
...
page 7 begins at  28672

Before page 7 are seven pages, 0 through 6. Its start is 7×4096=28672 bytes from the file start. If the record starts 120 bytes into page 7, its file address is 28672+120=28792. These offsets have different origins: one starts at the file, the other at the page.

Now insert a 512-byte file header while retaining zero-based page numbering. Page 7 starts at 512+7×4096=29184; the record starts at 29184+120=29304. A formula without its layout assumptions can be arithmetically correct yet point at the wrong data.

The disk-space layer can maintain a page-ID mapping and provide allocate, deallocate, read and write operations. Moving a page to another file can change the mapping while higher layers keep requesting the same ID. Logical consecutive IDs do not by themselves prove physically adjacent storage; the mapping and lower layers determine that.

Try: where does page 12 begin, first without and then with the header?

Without a header: 12×4096=49152 bytes. With a 512-byte header: 49664. Neither answer includes a record-relative offset until a record position is given.

Key takeaway

Identify each offset’s origin before adding offsets. The value 28672 is measured from the start of the file; 120 is measured from the start of the page. Confusing those origins points to the wrong record even when the arithmetic is correct.

Where does page 12 begin with a 512-byte file header?

512+12×4096=49664 bytes from the file start.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 26–28 (printed slides 27–28, 30). Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: A page count is not yet a performance claim
sections.html:
A colleague says: “The query reads 1,000 records, so it needs 1,000 I/Os.” Ask where those records live. If ten fit on each of 100 pages, a full uncached scan needs 100 page reads under that layout. If all 100 pages are resident, that phase needs no disk reads. If only one desired record sits on each of 1,000 different absent pages, the count can be 1,000. Record count alone cannot settle it.

After counting pages, ask how they are reached. Our HDD exercise read the same number of pages in both cases but paid different positioning costs. Nearby access is spatial locality. Reusing a resident page over time is temporal locality. The first can improve transfer patterns; the second can avoid transfers. Disk-space placement and buffer replacement address these different opportunities.

SSDs remove mechanical seek/rotation but still have physical constraints. As an explicitly simplified extension, suppose an application writes 4 KiB of changed data while the flash/controller work counted at a declared boundary writes 16 KiB including copied data. Write amplification is 16/4=4: physical bytes divided by logical host bytes. Flash erase blocks are coarser than program units; copying, erasing and wear management affect the cost. Extra CPU time is not “write amplification”. The exact ratio depends on device and workload.

Use supplied latencies for a model exercise. Slide prices, capacities and device figures describe their teaching context, not a current buying recommendation. For a real workload, measure cache state, placement, request sizes, concurrency and device behaviour rather than treating a page count as elapsed time.

Try: a query makes fewer page reads but runs longer. Is that impossible?

No. Its reads may be more random or slower, and it may perform more CPU work or wait for other work. A page-I/O model isolates one cost; explain its assumptions before comparing total time.

Do consecutive logical page IDs guarantee contiguous physical locations?

No. Allocation and lower storage layers determine physical placement.

quiz.question: Under the exercise’s model, how long does reading 200 contiguous pages take?
quiz.explanation: Seek time plus rotational latency is 7 ms. Transferring 200 pages takes 20 ms, giving a total of 27 ms under the stated assumptions.
